cf.title: pageinspect: validate line pointers before using them

input.subject: [PATCH] pageinspect: validate line pointers before using them

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: the thread shows reproducible crashes and out-of-bounds reads, and the cost falls only on pageinspect callers. The remaining points are fixable design questions at level 2. standards-compat-1 asks which header checks are needed for memory safety, maintenance-fit-2 asks for a stated scope, and maintenance-fit-1 asks for a shared helper. None of them would stop a committer from reading further.

brief.title: pageinspect: validate page headers and line pointers on raw pages
brief.problem: pageinspect functions that take a raw page as bytea can read outside the page image, or fail an assertion, when given a corrupt or crafted page. The author shows ASan heap-buffer-overflow reports and backend crashes for GiST, B-tree, heap and BRIN functions. The functions are superuser-only, so the author frames this as robustness for people inspecting damaged pages.
brief.proposed_design: 0001 checks each line pointer and B-tree posting lists before use in the GiST, B-tree and hash item functions, and turns an assertion on LP_DEAD pivot tuples into an error. 0002 adds verify_page_header(), using the header checks of PageIsVerified() without the checksum, and checks BRIN line pointers, BRIN and GiST stored values and GIN posting lists. page_header() still shows damaged headers.
user_visible_surface: New ERROR from the item functions on corrupt input, for example "invalid line pointer at offset 1 in GiST page".
bt_page_items() raises ERRCODE_DATA_CORRUPTED "invalid pivot tuple at offset %u: line pointer marked dead" where it used to assert or return NULL.
heap_page_items(), brin_page_items(), GIN and hash functions now reject pages whose header fails the new header checks.
page_header() still accepts a page with a damaged header.
author_claims: Without the patch, crafted pages crash the backend or trip ASan in GiST, B-tree, heap and BRIN functions.
heap_page_items() already guards line pointers, and the patch brings the other access methods to the same level.
This is a robustness fix and not a security issue, because the functions are superuser-only.
Normal output for valid pages is unchanged, and each fix comes with regression tests.
brief.thread_state: Greg Burd found the LP_DEAD pivot assertion and Yilin Zhang found a BRIN tuple-data overread; v4 folds in both fixes. No one has reviewed the overall approach yet, and CFbot reports v4 needs a rebase.
unclear: The material does not say whether the fix should be back-patched to supported branches.
v4 checks that BRIN and GiST values fit in the tuple but not what they contain, so the material does not say whether value decoding can still misbehave.
The author offers to share header checks with PageIsVerified() through a common helper, and no one has answered.
The thread does not say whether functions such as bt_page_stats(), bt_metap() or hash_metapage_info() get the same header checks.
The material does not say whether a valid but unusual page, such as a new all-zero page, now raises an error where it used to return rows.

objections.title: Whole-page header check takes item listings away from forensic users
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA investigating a damaged heap block runs heap_page_items() on a page where only pd_flags has a flipped bit, or pd_special is wrong. Before the patch the call returned the line pointers and tuples, which are still in bounds. After the patch it raises an error, and the DBA loses the data needed to salvage rows.
objections.argument: Message #2 adds verify_page_header() with the same checks PageIsVerified() makes and applies it to heap_page_items(), brin_page_items(), GIN and hash. Some of those checks, such as pd_flags or pd_special alignment, have no bearing on whether reading the line pointer array is safe. heap_page_items() already guards each line pointer (message #1), so this is a behaviour change for the main users of the function, who inspect corrupt pages on purpose. A committer would likely ask for clamping pd_lower and checking only fields that bound memory access, and would weigh this more heavily if the patch is back-patched, which the thread does not settle.
objections.author_must_show: Which header checks are needed to keep reads inside the page image, and why should a page that fails only the other checks raise an error instead of returning its items?

critic.reasoning: PageIsVerified() also tests pd_flags bits and pd_special alignment, which do not bound reads of the line pointer array. The thread does not say why a page failing only those tests should lose its item listing, and page_header() is not a substitute for it.

objections.title: The hardening contract for raw-page input has no stated limit
objections.failure_scenario: A user hands brin_page_items() or gist_page_items() a page whose stored values fit inside the tuple but hold a crafted varlena header or opclass datum. The type output function reads past the value and the backend crashes. Each such report then arrives as a bug against a fix that looked complete, and someone has to decide whether to back-patch it.
objections.argument: Message #6 says v4 checks that values fit inside the tuple but not what they contain. Messages #3 and #5 each found a new crash in a version that looked complete, which suggests the cases go further than the patch covers. The proposal does not say where the boundary lies: which functions must never crash on any bytea, and which stay best-effort. Without that boundary, every new pageinspect function and every new on-page format must add checks, and no test fails when one is missing.
objections.author_must_show: Which pageinspect functions does the patch promise are safe on arbitrary bytea, and how is value decoding through type output functions covered or excluded from that promise?

critic.reasoning: Message #6 says v4 does not check what stored values contain, and the thread does not say which functions are meant to be safe on any bytea. Step-by-step hardening is existing pageinspect practice, so this asks for a scope statement and does not count against the approach.

objections.title: Duplicated header checks can drift from PageIsVerified()
objections.failure_scenario: A later commit tightens or changes the header checks in PageIsVerified(), for example a new pd_flags bit or a new rule for all-zero pages. Nothing makes verify_page_header() in pageinspect change with it. pageinspect then rejects valid pages or accepts pages the server treats as corrupt, and someone finds out from a user report.
objections.argument: Message #2 says verify_page_header() repeats the header checks of PageIsVerified() without the checksum. It keeps a second copy in contrib. The author offers a shared helper in bufpage.c, and message #2 got no answer on it. With a shared helper, a change to the rules in one place covers both callers, and a reviewer has no second copy to miss.
objections.author_must_show: Would a shared header-check helper in bufpage.c, used by both PageIsVerified() and pageinspect, replace verify_page_header() without changing what either caller accepts?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 confirms verify_page_header() repeats the PageIsVerified() header checks, and the offer of a shared helper is still unanswered. The drift risk is small because these rules change rarely, but nothing ties the two copies together, so it stays a fixable design question.

refuted.title: Second copy of the PageIsVerified() header checks in pageinspect
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes the header rules in PageIsVerified(), for example a new pd_flags bit or a new page layout rule, and does not update verify_page_header(). pageinspect then rejects valid pages or accepts headers that the server treats as corrupt. Users find out when heap_page_items() errors on a healthy page, and nothing fails at build time.
refuted.argument: Message #2 says verify_page_header() uses "the same checks PageIsVerified() makes on the header", so the patch adds a second implementation of an existing core check. The author's reason is valid: PageIsVerified() also checks the checksum and needs a block number that a raw bytea does not have. That explains why the function cannot be called as it is, but it does not justify a copy. The author offered a shared helper in message #2, and no one has answered.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the header checks be split out of PageIsVerified() into a helper that both bufpage.c and pageinspect call, so the two cannot drift?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1. Both describe the same drift between verify_page_header() and PageIsVerified() and ask for the same shared helper.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patch hardens superuser-only functions against crafted bytea input; it adds no function or privilege.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The entry is tagged Bugfix, and the new errors on damaged pages would change behaviour in supported branches if back-patched.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: verify_page_header() repeats the header checks of PageIsVerified(), and each new on-page format needs its own checks.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which header checks in verify_page_header() are needed to keep reads inside the page image, and why should a page failing only the others raise an error?
Which pageinspect functions does the series promise are safe on any bytea, and is value decoding through type output functions inside or outside that promise?
Is the series meant for back-patching, and if so, how do supported branches handle pages that returned rows before and now raise an error?
Does a new all-zero page still return the same result from heap_page_items() and the other item functions as before the patch?
Do bt_page_stats(), bt_metap() and hash_metapage_info() get the same header checks, or are they safe without them?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the page layout code in bufpage.c and the index access method page formats that pageinspect decodes.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the new error behaviour on damaged pages, for any back-patch decision, and for follow-up crash reports on cases the checks do not cover.
committability.author_follow_up: The author folded two reviewer-found fixes into v4 and offered a shared helper, but v4 has needed a rebase since 2026-11-10.

priority.reason: The series fixes reproducible crashes in a tool used by a small group of superusers who inspect damaged pages, and it stays inside contrib/pageinspect. The two patches are about 36 KiB across six access method files, and each check needs someone who knows that page format.

provisional_note: Without the code, the exact fields verify_page_header() checks and which functions call it could not be confirmed. Whether value decoding can still read past a stored value also depends on the code.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow pageinspect's bt_page_stats function to return a set of rows instead of a single row
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch first changed pageinspect's bt_page_stats to return a set of rows covering a range of B-Tree pages, with a pageinspect version bump to 1.11. After review it added a separate function, bt_multi_page_stats, which takes an index, a starting block number and a block count.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane listed open issues before the patch could be committed: no documentation update, no simple way to ask for all remaining pages (a count one too large raises an error), and a regression test that depends on tuple layout. He then showed the test fails on a 32-bit machine. The author did not address this feedback, and Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback after four weeks of inactivity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This feedback has not been addressed and the thread is idle four
weeks, so I have marked this CF entry as RwF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pageinspect - add functions on GIN and GiST indexes from gevel
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Alexander Korotkov, Tomas Vondra, Ashutosh Sharma, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the gevel module's functions for GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes into pageinspect, with tests and docs. The functions show whole-index statistics, print the tree and its stored objects, and estimate GIN value counts and query matches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said the functions read the whole index, while pageinspect inspects single pages, so the code belongs in a new extension or should be rewritten as page-level functions. Peter Eisentraut also found that the patch no longer compiled and that the stats functions returned one formatted text value where they should return a row with columns. The author planned a new contrib module but posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback after three weeks of waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The proposed patch uses a very different approach, reading the whole index,
not individual pages. Why should it be part of pageinspect?

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
Reverted commit(s): Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 06f5295 as per issues with this approach, both in
terms of efficiency impact and stability.  First, contrary to the
single-item cache for transaction IDs in transam.c, the cache may finish
by not be hit for a long time, and without an invalidation mechanism to
clear it, it would cause inconsistent results on wraparound for
example.  Second, the use of SubTransGetTopmostTransaction() for the
caching has a limited impact on performance.  SubTransGetParent() could
have more impact, though the benchmarking of the single-item approach
still needs to be proved, particularly under the conditions where SLRU
lookups are stressed in parallel with overflowed snapshots (aka more
than 64 subxids generated, for example).

After discussion with Andres Freund.

precedents_retrieved.title: new diagnostic items for the dynamic sql
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds two PL/pgSQL GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS items that return the text of a dynamic SQL statement that failed to parse and the error position in it. Pavel Stehule suggested the more general names PG_SQL_TEXT and PG_ERROR_LOCATION.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stalled with no further review, and the author's email bounced by August 2022, so nobody was left to carry it. Tom Lane judged the last versions far too invasive for a use case that seemed hypothetical, because a re-RAISE already preserves the query text and position in the client error report. He recommended returning to a definition equal to the PG_DIAG_INTERNAL_QUERY and PG_DIAG_INTERNAL_POSITION fields, returning NULL when they are absent. The entry was returned with feedback in December 2022.

precedents_retrieved.title: brin: avoid errors processing work item following concurrent reindex
precedents_retrieved.summary: When autovacuum processes a BRIN summarize work item for an index that a concurrent REINDEX CONCURRENTLY has dropped, it logs an ERROR. The patch makes brin_summarize_range lock the index OID and use try_relation_open, so it discards the work item silently, or at most reports it at INFO level as vacuum_open_relation does.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled without agreement on the approach. Alvaro Herrera did not want every work-item handler to silently discard items whose relation is gone. He preferred a transaction-end hook that removes work items for dropped relations, but nobody wrote it and the hook had no clear place to collect the OIDs. In September 2021 he proposed pushing the small fix to all branches, but Justin Pryzby still asked why an INFO message would not do, and the entry was closed with no consensus.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This thread has stalled, and from the discussions there isn't consencus on how to proceed (if at all?), so I'm marking this Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix assertion failure in SnapBuildInitialSnapshot()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes an assertion failure in SnapBuildInitialSnapshot(), where the snapshot xmin was older than the safe xid from GetOldestSafeDecodingTransactionId(). It changes the locking in ReplicationSlotsComputeRequiredXmin() so that a concurrent call, for example from an apply worker, cannot overwrite procArray->replication_slot_xmin with an older value.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stalled for about a year with no agreement on the locking approach. Andres Freund was concerned about holding ProcArrayLock exclusively while iterating over slots, and Robert Haas asked for data on that cost and suggested making ProcArraySetReplicationSlotXmin() refuse to retreat the value. Nobody answered Robert's points, so the entry was set to Waiting on Author and then returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
ProcArraySetReplicationSlotXmin() could refuse to retreat the values,
perhaps? If it computes an older value than what's there, it just does
nothing?

precedents_retrieved.title: allow building trusted languages without the untrusted versions
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Peter Eisentraut, Stephen Frost
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an optional argument to the --with-perl and --with-tcl configure options so a build can include only the trusted or only the untrusted version of PL/Perl and PL/Tcl. For PL/Perl it first splits the trusted and untrusted handler and validator functions, and it adjusts contrib Makefiles that depend on PL/Perl.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that leaving out untrusted languages gives no real security gain, because a user who can create untrusted extensions can already reach the file system through COPY TO PROGRAM. Other reviewers agreed the patch does not by itself let anyone disallow file system access, as the first message claimed. Peter Eisentraut noted that packagers can already choose which files to install. The author said he would withdraw it, and the entry was closed as Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Someone who's gained the ability to issue CREATE
EXTENSION on untrusted extensions has already got all the privileges he
needs; leaving out a few extension files is at most going to slow him
down a bit on the way to full filesystem access.

precedents_retrieved.title: Harden against premature discarding of WAL segments in TAP tests
precedents_retrieved.summary: Mark Dilger proposed hardening TAP tests that break under a small max_wal_size or with wal_consistency_checking=all, because WAL segments they need get removed. The patch set used a physical replication slot in 015_promotion_pages.pl and contrib/bloom, adjusted the pg_basebackup tests, and re-enabled the disabled bloom test.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch set. Tom Lane found that the bloom test failed because it waited for the standby to write the WAL, not replay it, and his fix was committed together with re-enabling the test. The author then judged that committing the other changes at the same time could confuse the diagnosis of any new intermittent buildfarm failures.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The issues were intermittent on the buildfarm, and committing other changes along with what Tom already committed would seem to confuse matters if any new issues were to arise.

precedents_retrieved.title: Skip all-visible pages during second HeapScan of CIC
precedents_retrieved.summary: During the second heap scan of create index concurrently, the patch checks the visibility map and skips all-visible pages, because tuples inserted after the first scan can only be on pages with the VM bit unset. Its safety rests on VM bits being set only by VACUUM, which conflicts with CIC on the relation lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that the correctness of CIC should not depend on VM bits never being set concurrently under the SUE lock, since setting them in more places is a goal. Alternatives followed (a lock to detect a running CIC, or snapshot management to stop all-visible from being set), but the thread reached no design, so the author offered to withdraw the patch and it was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Thus I really don't want to
base the correctness of CIC - a relatively infrequent operation - on the
assumption that no VM bits can be set concurrenty due to the SUE lock.

This feature was using a process local map to track the first few blocks

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P6] and [P7] deal with checksum verification of page headers in base backups, which is a different feature, and neither row records a reason that could apply here. No thread message points to an earlier attempt at hardening pageinspect against corrupt pages.
Within the standards and compatibility angle, no new SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object or pg_dump state is added. The only contract concern is the stricter rejection of damaged pages.

The patch changes only how contrib/pageinspect reads a bytea page image in backend memory. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog column, wire message or exported API. The touched files are all inside contrib/pageinspect, and pageinspect.h is private to that module, so pg_upgrade, standbys, subscribers and extensions are not affected. Back-patching would change error behavior only, with no ABI break. Precedents [P6] and [P7] concern checksum checks in base backups, and neither records a reason that applies here.

The patch adds no new function, privilege or default, and these pageinspect functions stay superuser-only. It narrows what a crafted bytea can do, so a committer would see no new exposure from the security angle; back-patch handling is for other panel members.
No hot-path cost: the checks run only inside superuser-only pageinspect functions. The listed precedents record no reason, so none is cited.
No existing feature makes the pageinspect raw-page functions safe on corrupt input. amcheck verifies relations and does not check user-supplied bytea images, so the need itself is not already met.

No demand objection. The patch fixes backend crashes and out-of-bounds reads in a tool whose main use is inspecting damaged pages, and its cost falls only on pageinspect callers. Three people in the thread reproduced and extended the cases.
